newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus president tells foes to get ready to leave.
newsitem.headline: Belarus president tells foes to get ready to leave.

text.p: Hardline President Alexander Lukashenko on Monday told political opponents who accuse him of dictatorial plans to be ready to flee Belarus if he wins a referendum due to end on November 24.
"From November 25 we will put things straight and everyone will have to work," the defiant leader told supporters at a rally in the former Soviet republic's second largest city.
"Whoever doesn't want this will have to find another motherland," said Lukashenko, who is trying to boost his powers in the referendum.
"I am not trying to scare anyone but that's how it will be," he told the crowd of some 5,000, who waved red and green Soviet-era flags that he has reintroduced during his presidency.

Troops and police sealed off the central square of the city, situated 350 km (200 miles) southeast of capital Minsk, hours before Lukashenko stepped onto the podium erected at the foot of a huge statue of Soviet state founder Vladimir Lenin.

Lukashenko, who won presidential polls in 1994 on promises to fight corruption and ensure close and friendly relations with its Slav neighbour Russia, has since waged war against power rivals grouped around parliament.
The fighting reached a decisive stage after Lukashenko initiated a referendum on a new constitution that would sharply boost his powers at the expense of the legislature.
His power bid has sparked accusations that he is planning to impose a personal dictatorship in the country of 10 million.
The referendum, branded by parliament, the prime minister, the constitutional court chairman and the central electoral commission as illegal, began on November 5.
"They say I am trying to seize power," Lukashenko, tall and balding, told the rally. "What other powers do I need? I have enough power already. They must have gone crazy."

As Lukashenko, known for his oratory skills, delivered his speech, the mostly elderly demonstrators fiercely waved banners that read "Lukashenko is our hope!" and "Yes to the presidential constitution!"

Lukashenko, who has forced two of his nationalist foes to seek political asylum in the United States and who has snubbed court decisions and parliamentary resolution he dislikes, denied he was threatening democracy.
"What dictatorship are they talking about if we talk freely on the square with no tanks or armoured vehicles around," he said. "Dictators act in quite another way."

Lukashenko said that after the referendum he did not plan to dissolve the rebel parliament. He also reiterated his opposition to introducing private land ownership in Belarus -- a question to be posed in the referendum on parliament's insistence.
He said he saw two main priorities for the post-referendum period -- boosting exports to the West to earn hard currency to help struggling national finances and to revive the republic's agriculture.
But at the same time Lukashenko made clear that, regardless of the referendum's outcome, he would not surrender power.
"People gave me power not to let someone take it from me," he said. "I will not surrender power."
